summary: A National WWI Museum and Memorial web page on trench warfare on the Western Front, describing how artillery and machine guns forced armies to dig in and stalemate set in. It covers the harsh conditions in trenches, including mud, trenchfoot, debris, and the deadly no-man's land between lines. It closes with the approximate length of the trench systems.
one_line: Describes life in World War I trenches on the Western Front, including mud, trenchfoot, no-man's land and the scale of the trench systems.
key_facts: After the early war of movement in the late summer of 1914, artillery and machine guns forced armies on the Western Front to dig trenches.
Fighting on the Western Front ground to a stalemate, and over the next four years both sides launched attacks against enemy trench lines that caused horrific casualties.
Trenches in WWI were constructed with sandbags, wooden planks, woven sticks, tangled barbed wire or even just stinking mud.
Soldiers on the front lines lived mired in mud, and duckboards and sandbags were used to keep out water.
A British infantry soldier wrote, "The mud in Belgium varies in consistency from water to about the thickness of dough ready for the oven."
Trenchfoot was a common condition from constant damp that, if left untreated, could require amputation to stave off severe infection or even death.
Trenches became trash dumps containing broken ammunition boxes, empty cartridges, torn uniforms, shattered helmets, soiled bandages, shrapnel balls and bone fragments.
Trenches collapsed from the weight of the war and became long graves.
'No-man's land' was an ancient term that gained terrible new meaning during WWI, littered with tree stumps and snarls of barbed wire.
Soldiers charging across no-man's land faced a hail of bullets, shrapnel and poison gas, and were easy targets with enormously high casualties.
By the end of 1914, after just five months of fighting, the number of dead and wounded exceeded four million men.
The trench systems on the Western Front were roughly 475 miles long, stretching from the English Channel to the Swiss Alps, though not in a continuous line.
Soldiers in trenches easily became trapped or killed by direct hits from artillery fire.
